beats.text: Your A.I. agent searches the help docs, calls a tool, and still gives a customer the wrong delivery date.
Was it the search, the prompt, or the model?
Without a trace, you're guessing.
Fix found: Arise Phoenix.
Think of it as an X-ray for your A.I. app.
It's free to run yourself, with almost twelve thousand GitHub stars.
Add a few lines to your app, and it sends traces over Open Telemetry, an open standard.
Each request becomes a tree of steps, with timings and tokens for each one.
One. Find the broken step: which documents came back, which tool ran, and what the model was sent.
Two. Grade the answers. Ready-made judges check for hallucination, correctness and tool choice.
Three. Test a fix before you ship. Replay a traced call with a new prompt, or run a change over saved examples and compare it with the last run.
Now, the catch.
Its makers call it open source, but the server is under the Elastic License: free to self-host, but you can't offer it to others as a hosted service.
Login is off by default, so switch it on before anyone else can reach it. For real workloads, the docs recommend Postgres and a persistent volume.
And it moves fast: eight major versions this year.
It's for developers building A.I. apps and agents who want tracing and testing on their own servers.
If you need managed alerts and team dashboards, it's not built for that.
Want an alternative? Take a look at Lang fuse.
To try it, install it with pip, run phoenix serve, and open it in your browser.
What problem should we fix next? Tell us in the comments.
